summary:
Ulyanovsk Oblast stands under the Russian national framework, which applies in full and offers no regional deviation material enough to score separately. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. For a visitor this means an identity document carrying an outdated marker cannot be corrected before or during travel, so any police, hotel or transport identity check reads a mismatch.

The 2013 'gay propaganda' law carries administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The expanded statute reaches public expression that 'justifies' gender transition, and foreign nationals who violate it face arrest, detention and deportation; official national government warnings and the US State Department's Level 4 Do Not Travel advisory both address LGBT travellers directly.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation carries 2-6 years' imprisonment and organising 6-10 years under Article 282.2. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or displaying its symbols. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Enforcement operates inside Ulyanovsk Oblast. Citing an October 2024 OVD-Info report, the UK Home Office records that Ilya Zhuravlev, former head of the dialysis centre in Inza in the Ulyanovsk region, was detained in August 2024 on charges of participating in the activities of the extremist 'LGBT movement' (Part 2 of Article 282.2) and coercion of a person to act of a sexual nature (Part 1 of Article 133). In March 2025 a Ulyanovsk-region doctor, who faced a maximum of one year's imprisonment for alleged sexual coercion, was also prosecuted for 'involving' another man in the LGBT movement and received a three-year sentence.

The UK Home Office note assesses that openly LGBT+ people in Russia are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, with the state able but not willing to provide protection, and records at least 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024. Physical coercion is documented: BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was held for nine months at a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk and forced to take testosterone. The US State Department advisory carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers, and the UK Home Office affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume has risen alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines bringing more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over the two preceding years. The Guardian documented on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Deaths in custody and self-reports of degradation indicate what an arrest can lead to. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, quoting a St Petersburg queer woman who described herself as a second-class citizen after the designation.

Ulyanovsk Oblast's enforcement pattern is not distinctive; comparable extremism and administrative charges have been brought across the country, and Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ulyanovsk Oblast face the same document regime as the rest of Russia: gender markers cannot be changed, so a corrected foreign passport or a visitor's updated documents will not be mirrored domestically. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been unavailable since the 2023 legislation prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents.

Local enforcement has produced named cases. Ilya Zhuravlev, former head of the Inza dialysis centre, was detained in August 2024 on extremism and sexual-coercion charges under Articles 282.2 and 133. A Ulyanovsk-region doctor received a three-year sentence in March 2025 after being prosecuted both for alleged sexual coercion and for 'involving' another man in the LGBT movement.

The UK Home Office records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and Human Rights Watch counted 101 extremism-related convictions by 30 June 2025. Residents seeking protection have no domestic remedy under the Home Office's assessment: the state is able but not willing to provide it.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not source any Ulyanovsk Oblast-specific provision on public facilities, healthcare access for trans visitors, or local hate-crime sentencing enhancements; those questions remain unresolved here rather than absent. Whether the Zhuravlev case has concluded, and on what outcome, is not stated in the sources provided.

No source in this inventory addresses entry or visa screening for trans travellers at Ulyanovsk's borders or airports, including whether passport gender markers are checked against presentation at the point of entry. The claim that document mismatches are read at identity checks follows from the national ban on marker changes, not from a sourced incident in this oblast.

The UK Home Office note's page update date of 12 August 2026 postdates the June 2025 content cited; whether the substantive assessment changed at that update is not sourced.
